C0.quote: We propose a general model of repeated voting in committees
C0.note: Repeated binary majority voting in committees; equilibrium behaviour under qualified majority rules.

C1.loc: Section 5.2, Theorem 1, p.13; Section 6.2, Theorem 2, p.20
C1.quote: We now characterize the set of equilibrium payoffs in the repeated game.
C1.note: Main results characterise subgame-perfect equilibrium payoffs. Welfare comparisons of majority rules (the optimal rule maximising the highest equilibrium payoff) are also main results. Incentives to vote non-sincerely are analysed as equilibrium behaviour, not as a separate manipulation or strategyproofness result, so they are coded EQ rather than SB.

C2.1.value: vote; voting strategy vi(u) ∈ {0,1} (votes in favor or against the reform)
C2.1.quote: each agent i votes either in favor or against the reform

C2.2.quote: associates to any reform u a vote vi (u) ∈ {0, 1}
C2.2.note: The input is a binary yes/no vote on a single reform versus the status quo, aggregated by a qualified majority threshold m.

C2.3.quote: If enacted, the reform yields utility ui ∈ R to agent
C2.3.note: Cardinal utilities ui are drawn each period, separately from votes.

C2.4.quote: agents may be incentivized to vote against their preference
C2.4.note: Votes vi(u) and utilities ui have separate notation. Sincere voting is defined as vi(u)=1{ui ≥ 0}.

C3.1.quote: At the unique Nash equilibrium in weakly undominated strategies
C3.1.note: Even the stage-game sincere benchmark is derived as an equilibrium of strategic voters who could deviate, not assumed.

C4.1.note: C2.2 contains only OTH (binary votes), so the applicability condition is not met. In any case, utilities are primitive and votes are chosen given them.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.loc: Section 4.1, p.9; Section 6.2, p.20; Section 7.1, Theorem 3, p.24
C5.1.quote: the efficient rule de (.) accepts every good reform
C5.1.note: Results evaluate outcomes by expected utility, efficiency and Pareto dominance.

C5.2.quote: we denote the (common) expected utility attached to such a rule
C5.2.note: Welfare is computed from utilities ui, which are defined separately from votes.

VOT.quote_behav: Agents then vote for the alternative that maximizes their continuation utility.
VOT.quote_info: Our model assumes complete information in the stage-game
VOT.note: Utilities are publicly observed at each stage, while future reforms are uncertain. In the stage game, sincere voting is the equilibrium choice of strategic voters. Appendix B gives an incomplete-information example in which agents observe only their own utility.

DES.note: The optimal majority rule is a comparative-statics exercise; no designer agent is modelled.

C8.1.note: SPE is refined by Symmetry, Anonymous Histories and As-if-pivotal Voting. The stage game uses Nash equilibrium in weakly undominated strategies, and sincere voting is stated to be weakly dominant.

claims.quote: The model provides a rationale for the use of super-majority rules
the inefficiency of (super-) majority rules may be exaggerated
may explain the prevalence of supermajority rules

C9.1.note: Claims concern institutions and which rules are used.

C9.2.quote: Our model assumes complete information in the stage-game
C9.2.note: Needed assumptions are all stated explicitly as model assumptions: strategic, patient voters (discount factor); complete current-stage information; independence of reforms across periods; welfare measured as expected utility over held utilities.

C1.reason: The non-sincere voting incentives are analysed only through equilibrium characterisation, which is EQ; adding SB as a separate type is not warranted.

C3.1.reason: Voters are strategic in every analysis; stage-game sincerity is an equilibrium result, not an assumption of non-strategic voters.

C6.VOT.reason: Stage-game sincere voting is chosen as a weakly dominant strategy, so voters are strategic throughout rather than MIXED.

C8.1.reason: The paper explicitly uses weak dominance for the stage game in addition to NE and SPE.
